input:
This staffing review takes a closer look at the position in the quality laboratory, where a team of 4 full-time staff have been covering the workload with the help of overtime that ran at around 9% of paid hours over the course of last year. The question that the review sets out to explore is whether it would make sense to replace roughly half of that overtime with one additional hire, given that such a hire would come in at something like $64k per year once all of the fully loaded costs are properly taken into account.

On the surface, the proposal can look like a sensible one, because a permanent member of staff appears to offer a tidier and more predictable arrangement than a continuing reliance on overtime working. There is, however, a very important consideration that has to be weighed properly here, which is essentially the question of timing. A hire, once in post, is paid for the full year, in the quiet months just as much as in the busy ones. The overtime in this laboratory, on the other hand, is heavily concentrated into two distinct seasonal peaks, when the sample load tends to arrive all at once, and in between those peaks the team simply works its standard contracted hours. The practical consequence of this is that the laboratory would be paying $64k across the whole year for additional cover that is only really needed for a relatively small part of it. Decision-makers will therefore want to satisfy themselves that converting a cost which only arises at peak periods into a fixed annual cost is genuinely the right course of action in these particular circumstances.
target:
Overtime in the quality laboratory ran at 9% of paid hours last year, on a staff of 4 full-time analysts. The review tests one change: replace half the overtime with one additional hire, at a fully loaded cost of $64k per year. The case turns on when the cost falls, and on that point the figures are one-sided.

The hire is paid for the full year, in quiet months and busy months alike. The overtime is concentrated in two seasonal peaks, when sample loads arrive together, and between the peaks the laboratory works its contracted hours. A hire appointed against peak overtime is therefore paid through the quiet months for cover that the quiet months do not need, and the laboratory carries the cost at exactly the times when the load that justifies the cost is absent. The comparison is not between the hire and the premium bill for the overtime itself. That premium cost is a different figure, and the review does not rest on it. The comparison is between a fixed cost that runs in every month of the year and a variable cost that arises in two peaks and in no other month. On the figures given, the change converts a peak-only cost into a full-year cost of $64k. Whether the conversion is worth paying turns on the cost of a peak the present staff cannot cover, and that cost sits outside the figures this review was given.
